name: desire for social status
quote: One day I'm gonna be somebody.
description: Wanting to maintain or improve your perceived standing with a certain group.
perceptions: It's important to be perceived well by a certain social group.
I would like to stay in this group's graces or improve how they perceive me.
results: Seek a way to validate, preserve, or improve status.

guidance.description: Without status in some group perceived as powerful, we may not feel safe. It may worth understanding how your interest in a particular group is effecting your experiences.
One group that's important for many is the relationship with others of their own gender -- male bonding groups and female bonding groups.

otherVariations: desire to be perceived a certain way

comparisons.description: 'Desire for social influence' is trying to get people to see your way so they're more likely to help you somehow. With 'desire for social status', you're less concerned about a particular goal and more concerned with your group ranking. They are certainly related - you're likely to have more influence if you have a higher ranking.

variations.name: desire for validation
variations.description: Wanting to have your social value confirmed.
perceptions: I'm not sure where I stand with a particular social group.
I would like to confirm that my standing is still positive.
results: Seek a way to confirm approval from others.

guidance.description: If you find yourself seeking validation more often than healthy, consider seeking support resources.

variations.name: desire for unconditional validation
variations.description: Wanting to know that your social value is automatically confirmed by a certain person or group even if you make a mistake.
perceptions: It's tiring and stressful to have to constantly strive for validation.
There are certain people who should accept me without my having to do anything.

guidance.description: It's normal to get tired of the constant battle of social perceptions. We all want a few people who will accept us regardless of failures. Unfortunately, reality may be a little more complicated than that. It may be better to long for a 'highly tolerant love'.

variations.name: desire to make your mark
variations.description: Wanting to express your agency in a social context.
results: If you're trying to score social points, the result should be good for your group or bad for a rival group.

guidance.description: The desire to be seen is a reaction to feeling unimportant. Consider finding a way to make your mark in a slow positive way.

comparisons.description: When striving to look good in the eyes of a particular social group, the action needs to positive or neutral and display characteristics the group values. If you're doing something just to get attention, the results don't matter as much.

variations.name: desire to demonstrate skills
variations.description: Wanting others to see something you can do that's unusually good.
perceptions: I want to be seen doing this thing I'm good at.
desires: desire to be perceived a certain way
results: The results will need to be considered relatively positive or the attempt may backfire.

guidance.description: Some skills are easy to show off - just go out and do them. Others are harder to demo. Here are some references that may help.
Showing off becomes a problem when it is more than just seeking an occasional pat on the back for a well-done job.

variations.name: desire to win
variations.description: You want to win in a competition with another person or group.
perceptions: There's a competition that I'd like to win.
Winning it will improve my standing.

variations.name: desire for a valued asset
variations.description: Wanting to have access to something valued by a social group as a sign of social status, whether the asset is money, collectibles, fame, attractiveness, or something else.
perceptions: Having more of this asset would make my life better.
results: Seek ways to obtain an asset that scratches the itch.

guidance.description: Studies have shown over and over again that after a certain point, money does not buy you happiness (Kahneman & Deaton, 2010).

examples: Wanting to be able to pay your bills this month.
Wanting a fancy car to impress the neighbors.

variations.name: desire to impact negatively
variations.description: Wanting to annoy, scare, or harm a person or group for revenge, to control behavior, or to gain status with another group.
perceptions: I think negatively of some person or group.
It would be fun to see them irritated, scared, or harmed.
My social group will praise me for attacking them.
results: The results of your attack on the outgroup will depend on the nature of the attack and whether your in-group condones knocking others down to gain.
You may have a perception that you got the upper hand in the exchange.

guidance.description: If you're open to considering more pro-social behaviors, there are many resources online. They're probably more boring than whatever adrenaline-soaked content got you into antisocial behavior, but they may provide a more subtle and longer-lasting feeling. This doesn't suggest everyone should be nice. Just less antagonistic and more persuasive.

variations.name: desire to associate with high status people
variations.description: Wanting to have access to other people partly as a sign of social status, whether they are famous, powerful, attractive, wealthy, etc.
perceptions: Being associated with this person could raise my status.
examples: Getting yourself invited to an important meeting.
Wanting to have an attractive spouse.
Wanting to be in the 'cool' clique.

variations.name: desire to decrease others status
variations.description: A perception that relative status matters so knocking down others in your group will improve your own position.
perceptions: Someone else has a higher status in a group I care about.
They are imperfect humans, so I can find a flaw.
Lowering their status will make my relative status higher.
examples: False report about a co-worker to your manager.

comparisons.description: 'Desire to impact negatively' is focused on people outside of your group, while 'desire to decrease others status' is intra-group.

commentaries.quote: People sacrifice so many necessities of life to impress one another that they appear to be responding to a higher, spiritual need.
commentaries.attribution: Steven Pinker in 'How the Mind Works'

commentaries.quote: The deepest craving of human nature is the need to be appreciated.

If groups are fighting, it's about relative status. It's not really about the religion. It's not primarily about ancestry. It's not primarily about income, education level, or accent. These things matter because they sort people into groups, and people in these groups can feel threatened by rival group. And sometimes the grievances are even legitimate.
Gaining social status with one group probably involves losing status with another.
The problem - at least in the United States - is not that people can't find jobs. The problem is that they're no longer finding jobs that provide them with dignity and decent social status.

Status illegibility is necessary to keep a group of losers stable. It is a deep form of uncertainty. I am not saying that there is a ranking that is just not known or knowable. I am saying there is no clear ranking to be known.

We quickly and unconsciously measure social status for everyone automatically. The problem is that we each have different measuring sticks. Status can be based in different amounts of appearance, age, wealth, behavior, accent, gender, religion, group membership, or pretty much any other factor.

The brain can only handle a few absolute statuses: high, medium, and low. Some people want to be high status, some do not. No one wants to be low status, but the human brain insists that there must be members in the lowest bucket, even if they're not aware of their position. Within each bucket, we're sensitive about measuring fuzzy status differences relative to others, striving to maintain or improve our relative position.
The very rich and the very poor have so much in common... no one expects them to conform to social niceties. It’s only those of us in the middle who must constantly prove our worth to both sides.
